transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

I guess… I came in because things at work got really out of hand. I’m an industrial production manager, and I was suddenly starting all these plant redesign projects, calling suppliers after hours like it was totally normal, rewriting the whole shift plan by myself—honestly, I even thought I was making everything better.

And then it was like I couldn’t keep up with the mess I’d created. Or not mess, exactly, because some of it probably did need doing, but… you know how production schedules are, once you move one thing, everything else shifts. Anyway, I went from doing all of that nonstop to suddenly feeling like I was drowning in the plans I’d set in motion. That’s why I’m here.
During that time, were you needing much less sleep than usual and still feeling energetic?

Yeah. I mean, yes—definitely less sleep. I’d sleep maybe two or three hours, and then I’d be up before my alarm, already thinking about conveyor layouts or some vendor quote I wanted to revise.

The weird part is I didn’t feel tired. I’d get to the plant feeling sharp, kind of charged, like sleep was this optional thing that just slowed people down. Which sounds ridiculous now, because normally if I don’t sleep I’m useless, but at the time it felt… efficient, I guess. Like I’d found extra hours everyone else was wasting.
During that time, did you have any beliefs that other people said were unrealistic or untrue?

Yeah… I mean, people definitely acted like I was being unrealistic. I really believed I could fix the whole production workflow faster than the consulting team we’d brought in, which sounds arrogant when I say it now.

At the time it didn’t feel arrogant, though. It felt obvious. Like they were overcomplicating everything with these endless diagrams and meetings, and I could just… see the solution. I remember brushing off concerns from my supervisor because failure honestly didn’t feel like a real possibility. I was just sure I was right.
Have you ever had a period lasting at least two weeks when you felt depressed most of the day nearly every day?

Yeah… yes. It’s been more than two weeks. Honestly it’s been closer to three months now, this really heavy stretch where most days I just feel… low, like it’s sitting on me.

It got worse around the move and the new plant assignment, I think. Or maybe those just made it harder to hide—moving is always awful, with boxes everywhere and not knowing where anything is, and then at the plant there were all these little fires to put out, and I kept thinking if I could just get settled it would lift. But it didn’t really. It’s been there most of the day, nearly every day, for months.
During that high-energy period, were you hospitalized because of your behavior or mental state?

I don’t think so? I mean, no one took me to a hospital or anything like that. There were definitely people at work who were upset with me, and I remember my sister saying I sounded “wired,” but—sorry, that’s not what you asked.

No, I wasn’t hospitalized during that period.
Before this recent high-energy period, had you ever had another episode of depression at any earlier time in your life?

I’m… not really sure how to answer that cleanly. I mean, I’ve had rough times before, like everyone has, especially in school and early jobs—production schedules can just eat your whole life if you let them, and I was always the person staying late because I thought if I didn’t, something would fall apart.

But an actual episode of depression before this? I don’t know. I don’t want to say yes if it was just stress or being overwhelmed. Nothing is coming to mind clearly the way this recent stretch does.
During that high-energy period, did your behavior cause serious problems at work or in your daily functioning?

Yeah… it did. I mean, I kept trying to frame it as just work being messy, because shift planning is always messy—people call out, machines go down, somebody needs coverage, and then everyone acts like you personally invented the schedule to ruin their life.

But it got past that. I actually had to ask to be pulled out of a shift-planning meeting, which is… not like me, because that’s literally part of my job. And then occupational health got involved because I wasn’t really able to make the basic production decisions I’m supposed to be able to make. So, yes, it caused serious problems at work.
